Those protocols augmented the US-CERN cooperation agreement signed in May 2015 in a White House ceremony to confirm the US' continued commitment to research at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). It also officially expanded the US-CERN partnership to include work on a US-based research program and on the study of a future circular collider.

The US is the most represented nation in both the ATLAS and CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) collaborations at the LHC (will explain ATLAS and CMS). Its contributions are sponsored through the US Department of Energy's Office of Science and the Natural Science Foundation. The US will continue to support the LHC program through participation in the ATLAS, CMS, and ALICE experiments.

The LHC produces volumes of data that physicists must sift through to search for new discoveries. Thanks to planning and a pilot project funded by the offices of Advanced Scientific Computing Research and High-end Energy Physics within the Department of Energy's Office of Science, a data-management tool developed by physicists in the US is available to meet the big-data challenge. This workload management system is known as PanDA (Production and Distributed Analysis).

ATLAS is a particle physics experiment at LHC at CERN. In essence, it is a detector that is searching for new discoveries in the head-on collisions of extraordinarily high energy. It will learn about the basic forms that have shaped our Universe since the beginning of time, and that will determine its fate. Among the possible unknowns are the origin of mass, extra dimensions of space, unification of fundamental forces, and evidence for dark matter in the Universe. The CMS is a general-purpose detector at the LHC which has the same Scientific goals but uses different technical solutions and a different magnet-system design. The ATLAS experiment celebrated 25-years of service on October 1, 2017.
